title: Digraph: Loopless Arc Relation with Degree Definitions
content: The Digraph structure formalizes a finite directed graph with a bare arc relation adj : V → V → Prop and a loopless axiom ∀v, ¬odj v v. In-degree and out-degree are defined as cardinalities of filtered sets: outNeighbors v = Finset.univ.filter (adj v) and inNeighbors v = Finset.univ.filter (fun u => adj u v). isBalanced v := inDegree v = outDegree v. The design choice — not using Mathlib's SimpleGraph (undirected) or MultiGraph — is intentional: the directed case needs a custom definition since Mathlib's graph library focuses on undirected graphs.

title: Degree Sum via Fiberwise Decomposition: Σ outdeg = Σ indeg = |E|
content: sum_outDegree_eq_arcCount is proved by a bijection: the arc set decomposes as a disjoint union over sources — each source u contributes its out-neighborhood. Formally: Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise (f := Prod.fst) decomposes the arc set by source, then Finset.card_nbij maps (v ↦ (u,v)) ∈ outNeighbors u → arcs. The in-degree analogue groups arcs by target. Corollary: Σ indeg = Σ outdeg. This is the directed handshaking lemma — the foundation for the Euler criterion.

title: Circuit Necessity: Source/Target Permutation via Chain Property
content: The proof of directed_euler_circuit_necessary is the cleanest part of the file. Key insight: in a circuit walk (a.arcs.Chain' (fun a b => a.2 = b.1) + start = end), the multiset of arc sources is a permutation of the multiset of arc targets. Private lemma circuit_fst_perm_snd proves: arcs.map Prod.fst ~ arcs.map Prod.snd. The chain property gives map fst = u :: M and map snd = M ++ [u] (for the same M), and these are permutations via List.perm_iff_count + count commutativity of addition. Then eulerian_source_count bridges between list filter counts and degree definitions (via Finset.card_nbij). Since the walk is Eulerian (Nodup + all arcs covered), each filtered count equals the degree.
mathContext: Chain $\Rightarrow$ $(u::M, M{++}[u])$ perm $\Rightarrow$ multisets $\text{fst}\sim\text{snd}$; Eulerian $\Rightarrow$ count $v$ in sources $=\deg^+(v)$; conclusion: $\deg^-(v)=\deg^+(v)$

title: Path Necessity: Start/End Degree Asymmetry from Chain Structure
content: directed_euler_path_necessary proves the path analogue: an Eulerian path u→v implies outdeg(u)-indeg(u)=1, indeg(v)-outdeg(v)=1, and all intermediate vertices are balanced. The private lemma path_fst_snd_eq captures the path chain structure: [start] ++ map snd = map fst ++ [end]. This is the path analogue of the circuit permutation: instead of fst ~ snd (equal multisets), we have a shifted list identity. Compared to the circuit proof, the path case requires careful handling of the asymmetry at the start and end vertices. The sufficiency axiom directed_euler_path_sufficient asserts that these conditions are also sufficient (requiring Hierholzer's construction).
mathContext: Path chain: $[u]{++}\text{map snd}= \text{map fst}{++}[v]$; implies $\deg^+(u) - \deg^-(u) = 1$ and $\deg^-(v) - \deg^+(v) = 1$

title: Concrete Examples: Triangles, Squares, and Unbalanced Digraphs
content: Parts V–VIII instantiate the abstract theory on concrete small digraphs. The directed triangle (A→B→C→A) and directed square (cycle on 4 vertices) are verified to be balanced with native_decide, then serve as examples of Eulerian circuit candidates. The unbalanced triangle (A has 2 outgoing arcs, 0 incoming) shows the necessity of balance: unbal_no_euler_circuit derives a contradiction from directed_euler_circuit_necessary. The path example (A→B, B→C) illustrates the degree-imbalance conditions: A is a source (outdeg-indeg=1), C is a sink (indeg-outdeg=1), B is balanced. These serve as verification tests that the abstract definitions capture the intended structure.
mathContext: Triangle $A\to B\to C\to A$: $\deg^+=\deg^-=1$. Unbalanced: $\deg^+(A)=2, \deg^-(A)=0 \Rightarrow$ no circuit. Path $A\to B\to C$: $\deg^+(A)-\deg^-(A)=1$, $\deg^-(C)-\deg^+(C)=1$

title: de Bruijn Sequences: Eulerian Circuits in Overlap Graphs
content: Parts IX–X connect the Euler theory to de Bruijn sequences. A de Bruijn graph on alphabet Σ (|k| symbols) of order n has vertices Σ^{n-1} (length-(n-1) strings) and arcs Σ^n (length-n strings, with arc s’ pointing to the suffix of length n-1). An Eulerian circuit in this graph corresponds to a cyclic de Bruijn sequence of length k^n. deBruijn_arc_count proves |E| = k^n via exponential counting. symmetric_digraph_balanced proves any digraph with a symmetric adjacency relation is balanced — a useful sufficient condition. This connects Euler's theorem directly to combinatorics of sequences and the Chinese Postman Problem.
mathContext: de Bruijn graph: $|V|=k^{n-1}$, $|E|=k^n$; $\deg^+(v)=\deg^-(v)=k$ for all $v$; Eulerian circuit $\Leftrightarrow$ de Bruijn sequence of length $k^n$
